claim: MCF10A cells grown on Matrigel substrates proliferate from single isolated cells to form multicellular aggregates that polarize and clear the central mass of apoptotic cells through cavitation.
source: When MCF10A cells are grown on Matrigel substrates and in media supplemented with soluble Matrigel (Debnath et al., 2003), they proliferate from single isolated cells to form a multicellular aggregate, which then polarizes and clears the central mass of apoptotic cells, generating a central lumen in a process known as cavitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Debnath et al., 2003 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing the experimental observation.

claim: When isolated MCF10A cells are embedded in type 1 collagen gel, they proliferate to form elongated, solid cords of non-polarized cells.
source: In contrast, when isolated cells were embedded in a gel of type 1 collagen, which is the major ECM component in the stromal environment during mammary tubulogenesis (Schedin and Keely, 2011), they proliferated to form elongated, solid cords of non-polarized cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Krause et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schedin and Keely, 2011 and Krause et al., 2008, and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing experimental data.

claim: Type 1 collagen is the major ECM component in the stromal environment during mammary tubulogenesis.
source: In contrast, when isolated cells were embedded in a gel of type 1 collagen, which is the major ECM component in the stromal environment during mammary tubulogenesis (Schedin and Keely, 2011), they proliferated to form elongated, solid cords of non-polarized cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Krause et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schedin and Keely, 2011.

claim: MCF10A aggregates transplanted from Matrigel into collagen 1 gel spontaneously break symmetry and elongate to form cord-like structures.
source: Live-cell imaging revealed that the transplanted aggregates displayed small jiggling motions for several hours, then spontaneously broke symmetry and elongated to form cord-like structures similar to those formed when cultured in collagen from the outset (Figure 1B, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Elongating MCF10A aggregates are generally solid with no evident lumens.
source: These elongating aggregates were generally solid, with no evident lumens (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ki67-positive cells are more frequent in elongating parts of aggregates (41.00% ± 4.55%) compared with non-elongating parts (18.86% ± 3.05%).
source: Strikingly, Ki67-positive cells were more frequent in the elongating parts of the aggregates (41.00% ± 4.55% of all cells) compared with the non-elongating parts of the aggregates (18.86% ± 3.05%) (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from Ki67 staining shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The proportion of nuclei that divided is higher in elongating areas than in non-elongating areas within aggregates.
source: Live-cell imaging of cells expressing NLS-mCherry also showed that the proportion of nuclei that divided was higher in the elongating than the non-elongating areas within aggregates (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Increased proliferation is first evident in aggregates 2 days after transplantation.
source: More detailed inspection revealed that increased proliferation was first evident in aggregates 2 days after transplantation (Figure 1G) and appeared to precede the onset of symmetry breaking (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The symmetry ratio first increases at day 3, approximately 24 hr after an increase in proliferation is detected.
source: The symmetry ratio first increased at day 3 (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), approximately 24 hr after an increase in proliferation was detected (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: Ki67 positivity is twofold greater in elongating areas compared to non-elongating areas of aggregates that broke symmetry after 3 days of culture.
source: Ki67 positivity was twofold greater in the elongating areas (Figure 1I), suggesting that locoregional differences in proliferation were established early in the elongation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Elongation is inhibited when proliferation is blocked using mitomycin C and aphidicolin.
source: Importantly, elongation was inhibited when proliferation was blocked using the cell cycle inhibitors mitomycin C and aphidicolin (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with cell cycle inhibitors shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Cell proliferation is significantly reduced by mitomycin C (3.88% ± 1.18% at day 8) and aphidicolin (11.54% ± 3.55% at day 8) compared to control (26.63% ± 3.34% at day 8).
source: In control cultures, the proportion of Ki67-positive cells increased progressively after transplantation into collagen (from 2.28% ± 0.85% at day 1 to 26.63% ± 3.34% at day 8). However, cell proliferation was significantly reduced by mitomycin C (3.88% ± 1.18%, day 8) and aphidicolin (11.54% ± 3.55%, day 8) (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Aggregate elongation is significantly reduced by both mitomycin C and aphidicolin.
source: Aggregate elongation was also significantly reduced by both mitotic inhibitors (Figure 1J). Whereas the symmetry ratio increased as control anlage elongated, this was blocked by both mitomycin C and aphidicolin (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1J and 1L.

claim: Adding mitomycin C or aphidicolin after symmetry breaking (at 3 days) reduces elongation by approximately threefold.
source: To pursue this, we added mitomycin C or aphidicolin after the first signs of symmetry breaking were evident (at 3 days after transplantation). This reduced elongation by approximately threefold (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Cell proliferation is required for elongation, with the capacity to contribute early in the symmetry-breaking process and also later to sustain elongation.
source: Therefore, cell proliferation was required for elongation, with the capacity to contribute early in the symmetry-breaking process and also later to sustain elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that blocking proliferation at different time points affects elongation.

claim: Cells within elongating regions tend to divide along the axis of elongation.
source: Cells within the elongating regions tended to divide along the axis of elongation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), as revealed by comparing the axis of cell division and the principal axis of the region.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The angle difference between cell division axis and principal axis is smaller in elongating areas compared with non-elongating areas within the same aggregate.
source: The angle difference between these axes was smaller in elongating areas compared with non-elongating areas within the same aggregate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cells are motile within elongating aggregates.
source: Tracking also revealed that cells were motile within elongating aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The speeds of migration are identical in elongating and non-elongating regions of aggregates.
source: When we examined regional differences within aggregates that had undergone elongation, we found that the speeds of migration were identical in the parts that were elongating compared with the non-elongating regions of the aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The straightness of cell tracks is slightly greater in elongating areas than in non-elongating areas.
source: However, the straightness of the tracks, which was used as an index of the persistence of migration, was slightly greater in the elongating areas than in the non-elongating areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The track displacement angle is less in elongating areas than in non-elongating areas.
source: We measured this by comparing the orientation of the tracks with the principal axis of the aggregates (track displacement angle, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E). The track displacement angle was less in the elongating areas than in the non-elongating areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Inhibition of proliferation with mitomycin C or aphidicolin does not affect cell migration speeds in either rounded or elongated areas.
source: Inhibition of proliferation with either mitomycin C or aphidicolin did not affect cell migration speeds in either the rounded or elongated areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Blocking proliferation slightly reduces track straightness and increases the track displacement angle.
source: However, blocking proliferation slightly reduced track straightness, implying a reduction in persistence (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F) and increased the track displacement angle (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F and 3G.

claim: Re-embedded aggregates lose laminin V expression over time.
source: Consistent with the change in matrix environment associated with the transplantation process, re-embedded aggregates lost laminin V expression over time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aggregates express fibronectin throughout the experiments without any evident regional differences in the elongating areas.
source: They expressed fibronectin throughout the experiments without any evident regional differences in the elongating areas of aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Collagen 1 condenses around aggregates that have begun to elongate, forming dense bands that extend away from the cells into the gel.
source: Aggregate elongation appeared to coincide with change in fibril organization. Whereas fibrils appeared isotropic in acellular gels, collagen condensed around the aggregates that had begun to elongate, forming dense bands that extended away from the cells into the gel.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of collagen organization using CNA35 labeling.

claim: Collagen coherency increases with the increase in symmetry ratio after 8 days culture.
source: Then, we compared collagen coherency with aggregate shape, as measured by the symmetry ratio (Figure 2B), after 8 days culture, when elongation was established. Overall, collagen coherency increased with the increase in symmetry ratio (Figure 2C), implying that the degree of collagen bundling increased with aggregate elongation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Collagen coherency is greater in regions proximate to the elongating parts of aggregates compared with the non-elongating parts.
source: Furthermore, closer examination around elongating aggregates showed that collagen coherency was greater in regions proximate to the elongating parts of the aggregates compared with the non-elongating parts (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Aggregates that remain spherical show no regional differences in collagen organization.
source: In contrast, aggregates that remained spherical showed no regional differences in collagen organization.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of collagen coherency around non-elongated aggregates.

claim: Collagen 1 coherency increases around elongating areas as aggregates break symmetry in the first three days of culture.
source: Because aggregates varied in the timing of when they broke symmetry, we examined aggregates by live imaging in the first three days of the assays. We then subdivided these based on their symmetry ratio and compared the coherency of collagen 1 around the elongating areas of aggregates with that around the non-elongating areas (i.e., those that remained rounded, expressed as a fold difference). This showed that collagen 1 coherency increased around the elongating areas as they broke symmetry (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Collagen bundling requires cell proliferation, as coherency is reduced by treatment with mitomycin C or aphidicolin.
source: Collagen bundling required cell proliferation, as coherency was reduced by treatment with either mitomycin C or aphidicolin (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Collagen bundling is reduced when cellular contractility is inhibited with blebbistatin or Y27632.
source: Collagen bundling was also reduced when we inhibited cellular contractility with the myosin antagonist, blebbistatin, or the Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor, Y27632 (Figure 2H, I), consistent with reports that cell contractility can condense collagen (Brownfield et al., 2013; Buchmann et al., 2021; Gjorevski et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and I, and citations to previous studies.

claim: Collagen condensation persists around aggregates treated with NSC23766, which does not affect aggregate elongation or cell movement speed.
source: In contrast, collagen condensation persisted around aggregates treated with the Rac1 GEF inhibitor NSC23766, which did not affect aggregate elongation or the speed with which cells moved within the aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The collagen gel around non-elongating areas of aggregates shows a broad distribution of orientations relative to the axis of the aggregate.
source: First, we assembled histograms of gel orientation, setting the principal axis of elongation in the whole aggregate as 0o (Figure 2J). The gels around non-elongating areas of the aggregates showed a broad distribution of orientations relative to the axis of the aggregate (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The gel around elongating regions of aggregates tends to orient with the principal axis of the aggregates.
source: In contrast, the gel around the elongating regions of aggregates tended to orient with the principal axis of the aggregates.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of gel orientation shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The angle difference between the axes of collagen polarity and aggregate elongation is significantly smaller around elongating regions than around non-elongating regions.
source: We found that the angle differences between the axes of collagen polarity and aggregate elongation was significantly smaller around the elongating regions than around the non-elongating regions of the aggregates (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Collagen fibers become isotropically distributed in unstretched gels and become more coherent and polarized immediately after stretching.
source: Second harmonic imaging confirmed that collagen fibers were isotropically distributed in the unstretched gels and became more coherent (bundled) and more polarized immediately after stretching (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), with their principal axes oriented in the direction of stretch (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by second harmonic imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D, and E.

claim: Polarization of collagen fibrils can be preserved for at least 7 days after the application of stretch by re-embedding the collagen rings in a larger collagen gel.
source: Moreover, polarization of the collagen fibrils could be preserved for at least 7 days after the application of stretch by re-embedding the collagen rings in a larger collagen gel (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When gels are allowed to float in medium after stretching, gel coherency and polarity revert to that of unstretched gels.
source: In contrast, when gels were allowed to float in medium after stretching (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), gel coherency (Figure 3E) and polarity (Figure 3F) reverted to that of unstretched gels.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D, E, and F.

claim: Aggregates do not become elongated during the period when stretch is actively applied.
source: Interestingly, the aggregates did not become elongated during the period when stretch was actively applied. The symmetry ratios of aggregates immediately after stretching were identical to those in unstretched aggregates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Symmetry breaking occurs earlier when stretched gels are allowed to retain collagen polarization by re-embedding (35.14 ± 3.28 hr) compared with aggregates in non-stretched gels (68.40 ± 5.88 hr).
source: However, symmetry breaking occurred earlier when stretched gels were allowed to retain collagen polarization by re-embedding (35.14 ± 3.28 hr, Figure 3G and H) compared with aggregates that were allowed to break symmetry spontaneously in non-stretched gels (68.40 ± 5.88 hr, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The symmetry ratios of aggregates embedded in stretch-polarized gels are significantly greater than those seen with native gels.
source: Moreover, the degree of elongation was also enhanced once it had begun. The symmetry ratios of aggregates embedded in stretch-polarized gels were significantly greater than those seen with native gels (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Stretch-polarized aggregates elongate preferentially along the axis of the exogenous stretch, whereas aggregates in non-stretched gels elongate in a random direction.
source: Stretch-polarized aggregates also elongated preferentially along the axis of the exogenous stretch, whereas aggregates in non-stretched gels elongated in a random direction (Figure 3G and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G, J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D, and Video 2.

claim: The angle difference between collagen fiber polarity and aggregate elongation is significantly smaller in stretch-polarized gels than in unstretched control gels.
source: The angle difference between collagen fiber polarity and aggregate elongation was significantly smaller in stretch-polarized gels than in unstretched control gels (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Collagen gel reorganization is preserved in stretch-polarized gels and is oriented in the direction of the original stretch.
source: Of note, collagen gel reorganization was preserved in the stretch-polarized gels (Figure 3L and M), even in the presence of cellular aggregates, and this was oriented in the direction of the original stretch.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: Similar intensity of fibronectin staining is seen in stretch-polarized aggregates compared with controls, suggesting that fibronectin deposition is not stimulated by stretch stimulation.
source: In contrast, similar intensity of fibronectin staining was seen in stretch-polarized aggregates compared with controls, suggesting that fibronectin deposition was not stimulated by the stretch stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The proportion of aggregates that elongate after stretching is reduced when the gels are floated rather than being re-embedded.
source: Importantly, the impact of stretch on the aggregates was disrupted when collagen polarization was reversed. The proportion of aggregates that elongated after stretching was reduced when the gels were floated rather than being re-embedded (Figure 4A) and their length of elongation was reduced (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Cell-based forces cannot overcome the external forces acting on the gel as the reversal of collagen polarization occurs even when aggregates are incorporated into the gel.
source: Of note, cell-based forces could not overcome the external forces acting on the gel as the reversal of collagen polarization occurred even when aggregates were incorporated into the gel (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Stretch polarization stimulates cell proliferation.
source: Since cell proliferation was a major driver of spontaneous aggregate elongation, we then asked if it was altered when the collagen gel was polarized by stretch. Indeed, we found that stretch polarization stimulated cell proliferation (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in the proportion of Ki67-positive cells is evident at day 1 after stretch polarization, whereas it does not increase till day 2 in unstretched gels.
source: An increase in the proportion of Ki67-positive cells was evident at day 1 after stretch polarization, whereas it did not increase till day 2 in unstretched gels.
evidence: The claim is based on time-course data of Ki67 staining.

claim: The proportion of Ki67 cells is consistently greater in stretch-polarized gels during the early phase of culture (days 1–3) as well as at the end of experiments (day 8).
source: Moreover, the proportion of Ki67 cells was consistently greater in stretch-polarized gels during the early phase of culture (days 1–3) as well as at the end of our experiments (day 8).
evidence: The claim is based on time-course data of Ki67 staining.

claim: Cell proliferation mediates the enhanced elongation in stretched gels as both the length and symmetry ratio of stretch-stimulated aggregates are reduced by mitomycin C and aphidicolin.
source: Cell proliferation mediated the enhanced elongation in the stretched gels as both the length (Figure 5B) and symmetry ratio (Figure 5C) of stretch-stimulated aggregates were reduced by mitomycin C and aphidicolin.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Proliferation is not increased if gels are allowed to float, rather than being re-embedded, after stretching.
source: However, proliferation was not increased if gels were allowed to float, rather than being re-embedded, after stretching. Floating the gels reduced the proportion of proliferating cells in the aggregates overall (Figure 5D and E) as well as those specifically within the area of elongation (Figure 5F), compared with gels that had been re-embedded to preserve collagen polarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5D, E, and F.

claim: The proportion of ERK-activated cells is significantly greater in the elongating regions of aggregates that had spontaneously broken symmetry than in the non-elongating areas.
source: We found that the proportion of ERK-activated cells was significantly greater in the elongating regions of aggregates that had spontaneously broken symmetry than in the non-elongating areas (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data using ERK/KTR biosensor shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: ERK activation is especially apparent in cells at the surface of aggregates that are in contact with the collagen gel.
source: This was especially apparent in cells at the surface of aggregates that were in contact with the collagen gel (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No changes in nuclear Yap1 staining are detected that might indicate Hippo pathway activation in the experiments.
source: In contrast, although Hippo pathway signaling has been implicated in breaking the symmetry of epithelial organoids (Serra et al., 2019), we did not detect any changes in nuclear Yap1 staining that might indicate that this pathway was being activated in our experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C, and citation to Serra et al., 2019.

claim: FR180204 reduces cell proliferation in response to stretch polarization.
source: This notion was supported by finding that FR180204 (50 μM) reduced cell proliferation in response to stretch polarization (Figure 6D and E) and decreased the proportion of aggregates that elongated (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D, E, and F.

claim: FR180204 reduces the length and asymmetric morphology of aggregates that do elongate.
source: As well, the length (Figure 6G) and asymmetric morphology (Figure 6H) were reduced in those aggregates that did elongate.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: ERK1/2 is critical for collagen polarization to stimulate cell proliferation for aggregate elongation.
source: Thus, ERK1/2 appeared to be critical for collagen polarization to stimulate cell proliferation for aggregate elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that ERK inhibition blocks proliferation and elongation in response to collagen polarization.

claim: MCF10A cells express α2β1-integrin.
source: This class of integrins contains a number of collagen 1 receptors, including α2β1-integrin (Heino, 2000; Käpylä et al., 2000), which was expressed in our MCF10A cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B and citations to Heino, 2000 and Käpylä et al., 2000.

claim: mAb AIIB2 blocks the induction of proliferation in stretch-polarized gels.
source: mAb AIIB2 (15 μg/ml) was added as aggregates were transplanted into the collagen gel rings and replenished after 7 days. mAb AIIB2 blocked the induction of proliferation in stretch-polarized gels, the proportion of Ki67-positive cells being significantly reduced in AIIB2-treated cultures compared with controls (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: After 3 days incubation, 49.19% ± 1.61% aggregates start to elongate in controls, whereas less than 20% of aggregates elongate when β1-integrins are inhibited (17.86% ± 4.78%).
source: After 3 days incubation, 49.19% ± 1.61% aggregates started to elongate in controls, whereas less than 20% of aggregates elongated when β1-integrins were inhibited (AIIB2: 17.86% ± 4.78%) (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: mAb AIIB2-treated aggregates that eventually elongate remain shorter and less asymmetric than in the absence of AIIB2.
source: Moreover, even when mAb AIIB2-treated aggregates eventually elongated upon prolonged culture (comparing the proportion of elongated cells at 7 days with that at 3 days), these aggregates remained shorter (Figure 7F) and less asymmetric (Figure 7G) than in the absence of AIIB2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: The ability of stretch polarization to stimulate ERK signaling at early (day 2) and later stages (day 7) is reduced when β1-integrins are blocked with mAb AIIB2.
source: Finally, we asked if the ERK response required β1-integrins. Indeed, we found that the ability of stretch polarization to stimulate ERK signaling at early (day 2) and later stages (day 7) was reduced when β1-integrins were blocked with mAb AIIB2 (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: A β1-integrin-ERK pathway is responsible for stimulating epithelial proliferation.
source: This implied that a β1-integrin-ERK pathway was responsible for stimulating epithelial proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that blocking β1-integrins reduces ERK activation and proliferation.

claim: Locoregional cell proliferation is a striking feature of MCF10A elongation in the experiments.
source: These results lead us to conclude that a polarized collagen 1 matrix can promote epithelial elongation by stimulating locoregional cell proliferation. We infer this because (1) locoregional cell proliferation was a striking feature of MCF10A elongation in our experiments, whose loss was not compensated for by other morphogenetic processes.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: The pattern of proliferation within aggregates is critically influenced by the polarized organization of the surrounding collagen 1 matrix.
source: (2) The pattern of proliferation within aggregates was critically influenced by the polarized organization of the surrounding collagen 1 matrix.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental observations showing that collagen polarization affects proliferation patterns.

claim: Collagen polarization and cell proliferation interact to guide epithelial elongation.
source: Together, we suggest that these reveal an interplay between collagen polarization and cell proliferation that can guide epithelial elongation (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Inhibiting proliferation early in the culture process blocks branching morphogenesis in mouse mammary organoids.
source: Elongation was reduced when mitomycin C and aphidicolin were added from the beginning of the assays, consistent with earlier evidence that inhibiting proliferation early in the culture process blocked branching morphogenesis in mouse mammary organoids (Ewald et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ewald et al., 2008.

claim: Elongation is compromised if proliferation is inhibited after the elongation process has begun, a later dependence that was not seen in organoids.
source: We also found that elongation was compromised if proliferation was inhibited after the elongation process had begun, a later dependence that was not seen in organoids (Huebner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Huebner et al., 2016.

claim: Collagen 1 orientation induces mammary organoid branching.
source: Similarly, collagen 1 orientation has been reported to induce mammary organoid branching (Brownfield et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brownfield et al., 2013.

claim: Increasing fibril alignment in acellular collagen gels increases fiber stiffness and decreases pore size.
source: Increasing fibril alignment in acellular collagen gels was reported to increase fiber stiffness and decrease pore size (Riching et al., 2014; Taufalele et al., 2019), even in the absence of externally applied forces.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Riching et al., 2014 and Taufalele et al., 2019.

claim: In single-cell cultures, aligned collagen fibers are associated with larger focal adhesions than non-aligned fibrils.
source: Moreover, in single-cell cultures aligned collagen fibers were associated with larger focal adhesions than non-aligned fibrils (Doyle and Yamada, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Doyle and Yamada, 2016.

claim: Integrins sense changes in matrix stiffness.
source: This is consistent with the well-characterized role for integrins to sense changes in matrix stiffness (Giannone and Sheetz, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giannone and Sheetz, 2006.

claim: Cell migration is a key driver of branching morphogenesis.
source: Cell migration is a key driver of branching morphogenesis (Gjorevski et al., 2015; Huebner et al., 2016), and earlier experiments reported that the application of external stretch to collagen-embedded aggregates could promote elongation through cell migration (Brownfield et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gjorevski et al., 2015, Huebner et al., 2016, and Brownfield et al., 2013.

claim: The application of external stretch to collagen-embedded aggregates can promote elongation through cell migration.
source: Cell migration is a key driver of branching morphogenesis (Gjorevski et al., 2015; Huebner et al., 2016), and earlier experiments reported that the application of external stretch to collagen-embedded aggregates could promote elongation through cell migration (Brownfield et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brownfield et al., 2013.

claim: Cells can orient their patterns of migration when collagen networks condense and form bundles in 2D systems.
source: Studies in 2D systems have shown that cells can orient their patterns of migration when collagen networks condense and form bundles (Mohammed et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Anisotropic confinement can orient patterns of cell division in micropatterning experiments using 2D substrata.
source: Micropatterning experiments using 2D substrata have shown that anisotropic confinement can orient patterns of cell division (Théry et al., 2005), potentially by orienting tensile stresses (Campinho et al., 2013; Legoff et al., 2013), as would also be predicted to accompany stiffer, condensed collagen bundles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Théry et al., 2005, Campinho et al., 2013, and Legoff et al., 2013.

claim: The basement membrane thins substantially and is remodeled in regions of epithelial elongation, such as the tips of mammary or salivary gland buds.
source: However, earlier studies reported that the basement membrane thins substantially and is remodeled in regions of epithelial elongation, such as the tips of mammary or salivary gland buds (Harunaga et al., 2014; Silberstein and Daniel, 1982; Williams and Daniel, 1983), potentially allowing elongating regions of epithelia to engage with collagen 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harunaga et al., 2014, Silberstein and Daniel, 1982, and Williams and Daniel, 1983.

claim: Regional polarization of the collagen 1 matrix begins in response to anisotropies in force that aggregates exert upon their ECM via their integrin adhesions.
source: In conclusion, we propose the following working model (Figure 8): regional polarization of the collagen 1 matrix begins in response to anisotropies in force that aggregates exert upon their ECM via their integrin adhesions (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed working model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cell-based forces exerted through integrins can apply strain on collagen fibrils.
source: Cell-based forces exerted through integrins can apply strain on collagen fibrils (Brownfield et al., 2013; Buchmann et al., 2021; Gjorevski et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2016) and, consistent with this, collagen reorganization in our experiments was compromised by inhibiting cellular contractility.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brownfield et al., 2013, Buchmann et al., 2021, Gjorevski et al., 2015, and Hall et al., 2016, and experimental data.

claim: Collagen polarization stimulates further cell proliferation in adjacent parts of the aggregate to sustain elongation.
source: The consequent locoregional collagen polarization then stimulates further cell proliferation in the adjacent parts of the aggregate to sustain elongation.
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed working model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Polarized collagen networks can provide a structural memory of the initial axis of symmetry breaking, a relatively long-lived spatial cue that directs further elongation of epithelial anlagen.
source: This would allow polarized collagen networks to effectively provide a structural memory of the initial axis of symmetry breaking, that is, a relatively long-lived spatial cue that directs further elongation of the epithelial anlagen.
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed working model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Branched tubules represent one of the archetypal modes of epithelial organization.
source: Branched tubules represent one of the archetypal modes of epithelial organization (Iruela-Arispe and Beitel, 2013; Varner and Nelson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Iruela-Arispe and Beitel, 2013 and Varner and Nelson, 2014.

claim: In organs such as the mammary gland and lungs, networks of hollow epithelial tubes mediate the physiological exchange of gases, nutrients, and solutes between the body and its external environment.
source: In organs such as the mammary gland and lungs, networks of hollow epithelial tubes mediate the physiological exchange of gases, nutrients, and solutes between the body and its external environment (Chung and Andrew, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chung and Andrew, 2008.

claim: Epithelial networks are established by a complex morphogenetic process where tubules grow outward from their precursors until they are instructed to branch, after which outgrowth continues until the network is completed.
source: These definitive networks are established by a complex morphogenetic process, where tubules grow outward from their precursors until they are instructed to branch, after which outgrowth continues until the network is completed (Affolter et al., 2009; Andrew and Ewald, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Affolter et al., 2009 and Andrew and Ewald, 2010.

claim: In the trachea, lumens appear early and accompany the growth of tubules.
source: For example, in the trachea, lumens appear early and accompany the growth of tubules (Schottenfeld et al., 2010), whereas in the salivary and mammary glands tubules first begin as non-polarized cellular aggregates (or anlage), which then elongate as solid, multicellular cords before eventually forming lumens (Bastidas-Ponce et al., 2017; Nerger and Nelson, 2019; Tucker, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schottenfeld et al., 2010.

claim: In the salivary and mammary glands, tubules first begin as non-polarized cellular aggregates (or anlage), which then elongate as solid, multicellular cords before eventually forming lumens.
source: For example, in the trachea, lumens appear early and accompany the growth of tubules (Schottenfeld et al., 2010), whereas in the salivary and mammary glands tubules first begin as non-polarized cellular aggregates (or anlage), which then elongate as solid, multicellular cords before eventually forming lumens (Bastidas-Ponce et al., 2017; Nerger and Nelson, 2019; Tucker, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bastidas-Ponce et al., 2017, Nerger and Nelson, 2019, and Tucker, 2007.

claim: The decision to branch is a critical checkpoint controlled by developmental signals and cell-cell and cell-ECM interactions.
source: The decision to branch is recognized to be a critical checkpoint that is controlled by developmental signals and cell-cell and cell-extracellular matrix (cell-ECM) interactions (Goodwin and Nelson, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Goodwin and Nelson, 2020.

claim: The elongation of tubule precursors is a regulated process controlled by receptor tyrosine kinases and other signaling pathways.
source: The elongation of tubule precursors is also thought to be a regulated process controlled by receptor tyrosine kinases and other signaling pathways (Costantini and Kopan, 2010; Gjorevski and Nelson, 2010; Sternlicht et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costantini and Kopan, 2010, Gjorevski and Nelson, 2010, and Sternlicht et al., 2006.

claim: Type 1 collagen is often the dominant form of collagen during epithelial tubulogenesis.
source: One of the main components of ECM is collagen, particularly type 1 collagen (also called collagen 1), which is often the dominant form during epithelial tubulogenesis (Graham et al., 1988; Keely et al., 1995; Llacua et al., 2018; Nakanishi et al., 1986; Simon-Assmann et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Graham et al., 1988, Keely et al., 1995, Llacua et al., 2018, Nakanishi et al., 1986, and Simon-Assmann et al., 1995.

claim: Fibrillar collagen helps scaffold other molecules, such as other ECM proteins and growth factors.
source: Fibrillar collagen helps scaffold other molecules, such other ECM proteins and growth factors (Kanematsu et al., 2004; Wipff and Hinz, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kanematsu et al., 2004 and Wipff and Hinz, 2008.

claim: Adhesion between cells and ECM allows the chemical and mechanical properties of the ECM to regulate cell signaling and gene regulation.
source: Adhesion between cells and ECM allows the chemical and mechanical properties of the ECM to regulate cell signaling and gene regulation (Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shi et al., 2011.

claim: Cell-ECM adhesions allow cell-based forces to reorganize the ECM.
source: These cell-ECM adhesions also allow cell-based forces to reorganize the ECM. In particular, cells can rearrange collagen fibrils to influence cell migration (Buchmann et al., 2021; Gjorevski et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buchmann et al., 2021, Gjorevski et al., 2015, Guo et al., 2012, and Shi et al., 2014.

claim: Fibrillar components of the ECM, such as collagen 1, are relatively long-lived.
source: Importantly, fibrillar components of the ECM, such as collagen 1, are relatively long-lived (Price and Spiro, 1977; Verzijl et al., 2000), making them attractive candidates to bridge time scales during the elongation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Price and Spiro, 1977 and Verzijl et al., 2000.

claim: Rearrangement of collagen has been implicated in patterning epithelial branching.
source: Indeed, rearrangement of collagen has been implicated in patterning epithelial branching (Brownfield et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2012; Harunaga et al., 2011; Ingman et al., 2006; Patel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brownfield et al., 2013, Guo et al., 2012, Harunaga et al., 2011, Ingman et al., 2006, and Patel et al., 2006.
